clinicalPearls: Bladder pain syndrome is chronic pelvic pain, pressure or discomfort perceived to relate to the bladder, accompanied by urinary frequency and urgency, in the absence of infection or other identifiable cause.
The defining feature that distinguishes it from overactive bladder is pain or discomfort that worsens with bladder filling and is relieved, at least transiently, by voiding.
It is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring confident elimination of infection, malignancy, carcinoma in situ, stones and other treatable pelvic pathology.
Cystoscopy with hydrodistension identifies a phenotype with Hunner lesions, which behaves differently and responds to lesion-directed treatment, distinct from the non-Hunner phenotype.
Glomerulations after hydrodistension are non-specific and are not sufficient alone to confirm the diagnosis.
It frequently overlaps with other chronic pain and functional conditions such as fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome and chronic pelvic pain, favouring a multidisciplinary approach.

Management is stepwise: education, dietary and stress modification, pelvic floor physical therapy and oral agents, escalating to intravesical therapy, and reserving major surgery for refractory disease.
Long courses of empirical antibiotics are inappropriate once infection has been excluded and should be avoided.
reference.pathophysiology: Bladder pain syndrome is understood as a multifactorial disorder rather than a single disease, with several interacting mechanisms proposed. A defective urothelial glycosaminoglycan layer is thought to increase urothelial permeability, allowing urinary potassium and other solutes to penetrate the bladder wall and irritate sensory nerves and detrusor muscle. Mast cell activation and neurogenic inflammation amplify the response, while peripheral and central sensitisation of afferent pathways lowers the pain threshold and helps explain the frequent overlap with other chronic pain syndromes. In the Hunner lesion phenotype there is a distinct picture of localised chronic inflammation with epithelial denudation and a dense inflammatory infiltrate. Reduced functional bladder capacity, autoimmune and microvascular contributions, and psychosocial factors that modulate pain perception are also implicated. No single mechanism accounts for all cases, and the clinical presentation reflects a combination of bladder-centred and systemic processes.
additionalDifferentials: Recurrent or chronic urinary tract infection
Carcinoma in situ of the bladder
Endometriosis and other gynaecological pelvic pain
Pelvic floor myofascial pain and chronic pelvic pain syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Urinalysis and culture, including tests for fastidious organisms where indicated
Urine cytology to help exclude carcinoma in situ
Frequency-volume bladder diary documenting small voided volumes
Cystoscopy with hydrodistension to identify Hunner lesions and capacity
Bladder biopsy where malignancy or Hunner lesion needs confirmation
Pelvic imaging or gynaecological assessment to exclude other pelvic pathology
redFlags: Visible haematuria requiring exclusion of malignancy
Positive or suspicious urine cytology suggesting carcinoma in situ
A history of pelvic irradiation or ketamine use pointing to a specific cystitis
Sterile pyuria that may indicate genitourinary tuberculosis
Rapidly worsening symptoms or systemic features atypical for the syndrome
reference.prognosis: Bladder pain syndrome is typically chronic and relapsing, and most patients require ongoing, individualised management rather than achieving cure; symptom control and preserved quality of life are realistic goals. The Hunner lesion phenotype often responds well to lesion-directed treatment, whereas widespread central sensitisation predicts a more refractory course.
pitfalls: Diagnosing the syndrome without adequately excluding infection, malignancy and carcinoma in situ
Missing a treatable Hunner lesion by omitting cystoscopy in a patient with persistent pain
Over-relying on non-specific glomerulations to confirm the diagnosis
Prescribing repeated empirical antibiotic courses after infection has been excluded
Neglecting pelvic floor dysfunction and coexisting chronic pain conditions that need concurrent treatment
references: European Association of Urology Guidelines on chronic pelvic pain
American Urological Association Guideline on interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome
management: A stepwise, phenotype-directed approach beginning with conservative measures — dietary modification, bladder training, stress management and pelvic-floor physiotherapy
Oral agents such as amitriptyline, pentosan polysulfate or antihistamines for symptom control
Intravesical instillation therapy, for example lidocaine, dimethyl sulfoxide or glycosaminoglycan-replacement agents, for refractory bladder symptoms
Lesion-directed treatment of Hunner lesions by fulguration, resection or intralesional corticosteroid injection
Escalate refractory disease to neuromodulation, intradetrusor botulinum toxin, immunomodulation with ciclosporin, or rarely reconstructive or cystectomy surgery
Manage overlapping chronic pain and functional conditions and analgesia within a multidisciplinary framework
